claims.statement: The homelab bring-up runbook is a from-scratch, phase-ordered procedure for a single headless host whose phases assume the prior phase's state (e.g. the two service users and their networks/volumes must exist before Forgejo or the app stacks are deployed), so a partial rebuild cannot skip ahead; it provisions Ubuntu Server LTS with firmware virtualization/IOMMU enabled and full-disk LVM, then hardens SSH to key-only, sets ufw default-deny inbound, and reaches the host over Tailscale only.

The host runs two unprivileged service users (`ci` and `prod`), each with its own rootless dockerd at its own socket and its own data root under its home, and the rootful docker.service is disabled — this is the isolation boundary that keeps a CI breakout from reaching prod or the host as root. The prod daemon hosts the long-lived services (Forgejo, Komodo, the RustFS-backed Nx cache, monitoring), while the CI daemon runs build/test jobs.

Rootless Docker must be installed for each service user from a `machinectl shell <user>@` session (`systemd-container` provides it), not `sudo -iu`/`su`: the setup tool needs a real systemd user session to install the auto-start unit, and the wrong session type silently falls back to a manual-start mode (it prints "systemd not detected" and points XDG_RUNTIME_DIR at the user's home instead of /run/user/<uid>). Linger must be enabled so the user manager and daemons run without an active login.

Each service user must have exactly one non-overlapping subordinate UID/GID range; `useradd -m` already assigns one, so the normal action is verification only. Adding a second range via `usermod --add-subuids` creates an overlap that breaks rootless Docker's user-namespace mapping with an opaque `newuidmap: write to uid_map failed: Invalid argument` error.

Cgroup delegation must be enabled at the systemd `user@.service` level (`Delegate=cpu cpuset io memory pids` via a drop-in, then reboot); otherwise rootless Docker only enforces memory/pids limits and silently ignores CPU/IO limits, which breaks the CI-vs-prod performance isolation that host cgroup caps on the user slices provide.

Although the two rootless daemons are isolated at the daemon and filesystem level, they still publish into the same host's port space, which is the origin of the prod↔CI port-collision class: a prod bind on 0.0.0.0 collides with a CI bind on the same port regardless of the CI host_ip, which is why prod admin/UI ports live in a reserved range enforced by the required `check-prod-ci-port-collision.mjs` guardrail.

This forge build (15.0.3+gitea-1.22.0) exposes no Actions-artifact API — `GET /api/v1/repos/.../actions/artifacts` is a missing route (404), not an empty result — so an `upload-artifact` APK is retrievable only by a human through the run page and only until it expires. `cd-deploy`'s `prod-apk` job therefore publishes every release APK to the generic package registry as package `mcm-app-android`, version `<expo.version>-<sha7>`, alongside a `.apk.sha256` sidecar in `sha256sum -c` format, using the existing `write:package` CI push token (no new token, no widened scope); retrieval uses a `read:package` token against `/api/packages` (not `/api/v1`).

Release-APK retention is count-based, not time-based: the measured universal release APK is 114,365,972 bytes (109 MB) on run #6036 and every deploy produces one, so `publish-apk.mjs` prunes to the newest 5 versions by `created_at` (≈550 MB ceiling) rather than a 30-day window, because a quiet month would delete every installable APK while a busy week would keep more than the disk affords. A version whose name ends in `-keep` is never pruned and does not consume a retention slot, which is the supported way to make a build outlive the window. The pruning keeps a version whose `created_at` fails to parse (deleting on a parse failure is the destructive direction), sorts by `created_at` rather than name (`1.10.0` sorts before `1.9.0` as a string, so name order would prune the newest first), and paginates the version listing because the forge defaults to 30 items ordered by name, making an unpaginated call a silent retention no-op.

`prod-apk` is deliberately non-blocking: no job `needs:` it, the publish step is `continue-on-error`, and `publish-apk.mjs` always exits 0 while printing `::error::` on every failure path, so a registry hiccup is visible in the job log without turning a deploy red. A re-upload of an already-published version is a 409 treated as "already published" rather than a failure, because the bytes are the same build of the same source.

The forge's `ubuntu-latest` runner label maps to `docker://node:22-bookworm`, a plain Node image running as root — not a GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runner — so GitHub-hosted-runner recipes do not transfer. In particular `sudo` is not installed and is unnecessary (the kvm runner executes as the unprivileged `ci` user, which also has no sudo), and a copied `sudo …` line dies on its first word; with a customary `|| true` the step goes green having done nothing, which is exactly what `cd-deploy`'s `prod-apk` disk step did on every run it ever made.

Dropping `sudo` from the disk step is worse than leaving the no-op: measured 2026-09-15 with `docker run --rm node:22-bookworm`, `/usr/share/dotnet`, `/opt/ghc`, `/usr/local/.ghcup`, `/usr/share/swift` and `/usr/local/share/powershell` do not exist, and the one sizeable removable directory, `/usr/local/lib/node_modules` (19 MB), holds `corepack` and `npm`, which `pnpm/action-setup` resolves pnpm through two steps later — so a working `rm -rf` would break the job to reclaim 19 MB, and would not even reclaim that, since deleting files in an image's lower layers writes whiteouts to the container layer and host usage goes UP. Freeing real host disk from a job means pruning the rootless daemon (`docker image prune -af`, no privileges needed), which `app-e2e`, `dast` and `build-deploy` do; `prod-apk` has no Docker CLI and nothing to prune.

`scripts/__tests__/prod-apk-disk-step.guard.test.mjs` pins the disk-step fix in both directions: it fails any workflow step anywhere in `.forgejo/workflows` that invokes `sudo` in command position, and it fails the `prod-apk` disk step if it deletes `/usr/local/lib/node_modules`, attempts any `rm`, or carries a `|| true` — requiring instead that the step state in its output that no reclamation is attempted and that its name not promise one. It further asserts the commit-status recorder exists, posts under its own context, is `always()` + `continue-on-error`, is off pull requests, reports `<unset>` rather than a wrong value, and matches none of `main`'s required status globs so it cannot gate a merge.

Forgejo runs on the prod daemon (a long-lived service, with Postgres behind it) as the source-of-truth forge, with Actions and the OCI/generic package registry enabled by env; GitHub is a downstream push mirror rather than the source. Every automated consumer authenticates with its own minimally-scoped named personal access token — registry push and pull are split, CD's git write uses a whitelisted-user PAT rather than the runner's auto token (which the pre-receive hook declines on protected `main`), and the debug dispatch token is revoked when idle.

Komodo provides CD to the prod daemon as Core + a Periphery agent + a database, using FerretDB rather than MongoDB (the unpinned Mongo image crash-loops on this new-kernel + rootless combination) and with Periphery repointed at the prod rootless socket. Its webhook is a git-style branch redeploy validated by HMAC with the global webhook secret — it will not consume a posted image digest — so promotion is digest-by-git: CI resolves the immutable digest, commits it to a tracked env file, pushes, then fires the signed webhook, and there is no rollback endpoint (rollback = redeploy the prior digest).

Every literal in the server-setup runbook is a placeholder, and the repository's topology-scrub and secret-scan gates fail the build if a real tailnet host, domain, IP or credential-shaped string lands in git; the runbook also warns that the host-level disaster-recovery snapshot of every stateful service is a different thing from the application's per-user collection backups, with neither replacing the other.

Reboot resilience (Phase 17) is enforced as config-as-code rather than by prose: `scripts/check-prod-restart-policy.mjs` requires `restart: always` on every long-running service in the prod compose files, forbids `restart: unless-stopped` (which does not bring a cleanly stopped container back after a reboot, because the graceful-shutdown drain unit leaves every container at `Exited (0)`), and allows `no`/`on-failure` only for name-matched one-shot containers. The gate runs selftest + scan as the "Prod restart-policy gate" step of the `naming` job in `.forgejo/workflows/guardrails.yml`, so a future prod service added with the obvious `unless-stopped` default cannot silently reintroduce the outage.

Production stack definitions and their deploy order are config-as-code: `infrastructure-as-code/komodo/stacks.toml` holds seven `[[stack]]` blocks that a single Komodo ResourceSync diff-applies, and each block carries `deploy = true` plus an `after` list so applying the sync also *deploys* them in dependency order — `prod-auth` as root, then `prod-mc-service` (waits on Keycloak JWKS), `prod-mcm-bff`, then `prod-movie-assistant` (agents last, since `spreadsheet-mcp` needs the BFF's network and Redis), with `prod-audit` independent, `prod-observability` ordered after the BFF for graph cleanliness only, and `prod-vault` hanging off `prod-auth`.

The Komodo ResourceSync does not create the production stacks from scratch: all four core stacks were created manually during Phase 15 (and the `prod-app → prod-mcm-bff` rename was also done by hand), so the first sync *adopts* the already-live stacks in place as a config diff, which is why the diff is previewed before the first apply.

The emulator job reaches `/dev/kvm` by executing directly on the ci host through a host-type Forgejo runner label defined as `kvm:host` (`runs-on: kvm` uses the label *name*), not by passing the device into a job container — that was the setup only until commit `235f2f4c`. What must therefore hold is host state: KVM enabled on the host, the `ci` user in the `kvm` group, and the runner still advertising the label. On this host `/dev/kvm` is mode 666 (`crw-rw-rw- root kvm`, measured 2026-10-12); 660 via a udev rule is the tighter option, and the group membership is what keeps the job working if it is applied. A host job must also provision its own Docker CLI and prove it reaches the `ci` rootless daemon at the job's `DOCKER_HOST` with no fallback socket, and a missing `/dev/kvm` fails the job loudly rather than skipping the mobile suite.

Phase 9 of the server-setup runbook bootstraps `PERIPHERY_ROOT_DIRECTORY` onto persistent disk (a directory under the `prod` user's home) instead of Komodo's stock `/etc/komodo` default, because under rootless Docker `/etc` is copy-up'd to a per-daemon tmpfs: a default Periphery root is wiped on every reboot along with the cloned repo checkout that every stack's relative bind-mounts resolve against, after which Docker auto-creates each missing bind-mount source *file* as a directory and the Mongo and Vault containers fail with `not a directory` (exit 127). Bootstrapping the persistent value at install time is what keeps a rebuild from reintroducing the tmpfs default.

Phase 8's self-hosted Nx remote cache is the open-source Rust `nx-cache-server` binary run as a `prod`-user systemd-user service (like the Actions runner), implementing Nx's built-in custom remote-cache-server API (Nx ≥ 20.8) because the first-party `@nx/s3-cache` / `@nx/shared-fs-cache` packages were deprecated over an unpatchable CVE and must not be used. Its backing S3 object store is RustFS (feature 080), deployed from a host-managed compose under the `prod` user's home on the same pinned image the git-tracked observability stack uses — a pin that must be copied by hand because Renovate never sees the host-managed file — running as the image's own uid, logging to stdout, with the console disabled and only the S3 port published, plus a one-shot init container that PUTs the cache bucket. Client wiring is entirely env-driven (a Forgejo variable for the server URL and a Forgejo secret for the access token, no `nx.json` literal), so local runs without the token fall back to the local cache and no remote-cache config leaks into the repo.

Moving the existing Nx-cache store to RustFS was an in-place, verified copy driven by `scripts/object-store-migration.sh` in ordered stages (`manifest` against the old store's endpoint → `inventory` → `copy --apply` from the old volume to the new → `verify` for parity), with the cache server stopped as the only writer, a one-line rollback (stop the new service, bring the old store up, restore its credentials), and recreating the cache empty accepted as an alternative because the data is rebuildable — a cold cache costs time, not correctness. That machinery has since been deleted, so the runbook's Phase 8 procedure is now the historical record of how it was done rather than an executable recipe, and the same tool carried the Langfuse object-store cutover.

The RustFS Nx-cache store is host-managed state, so it has a Renovate blind spot and a host-state trap: its compose lives under the `prod` user's home (like Forgejo, Komodo, cloudflared, beszel, dozzle and uptime-kuma), which Renovate does not see, so its image pin must be copied by hand from the git-tracked RustFS instance in the observability stack whenever that moves; its volume and network names are likewise host state that must be confirmed by ownership *and* contents; and the host backup script captures each store's config directory (never its data volume), which is why the live store's directory is on that path list.

The Nx-cache store cutover was performed on prod on 2026-10-21 (spec 080 T044) as a copy rather than a recreate, and the tool's `verify` stage reported 1360 → 1360 objects. The host facts the runbook records alongside it — the previous store's compose project, service, network and volume names, its access key, and the env-file key its secret lived under — are host state that exists nowhere in git. The retired store itself was then removed on 2026-10-24/25 (spec 080 T047, item #826) when the rollback window closed early, so those facts now describe a store that no longer exists on the host.

The tracked host backup script's `restic backup` path list names the service config directories `"$HOME/forgejo" "$HOME/komodo" "$HOME/rustfs" "$HOME/nx-cache"`. The retired object store's directory is **not** on it, and the runbook's Phase 8 sentence that once kept it there until the deferred cleanup is now inside a `<!-- history:begin -->` block: the cleanup (spec 080 T047, 2026-10-24/25) removed `/home/prod/minio/` with a matching `backup.sh` line, so the earlier runbook-versus-tracked-script disagreement is resolved in the script's favour. The store's data volume is deliberately never captured by either: it is rebuildable, and only the config directory is needed to stand the service back up.

The Nx-cache store's access/secret pair lives in two files that must change together: the store's own `.env`, and the cache server's env file, which carries the same pair as its `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`. On this host that env file's endpoint and bucket name were already correct, so the cutover changed only those two credential lines — leaving them behind yields a cache server that starts healthy and cannot read the store.

The Nx-cache store's volume is declared `external: true` under the explicit name `nx-cache-rustfs-data`, so compose never creates it: the now-deleted migration tool's `copy --apply` used to bring it into existence on a host that already held data, and on a new host with no prior data it is created empty with an explicit `docker volume create nx-cache-rustfs-data`. Referencing it before it exists aborts the compose up with an `external volume … not found` error and creates **no** containers, so the volume must exist before anything mounts it — the deploy fails rather than starting on an empty store.

Two env-file reading traps apply to the store cutover: each store's secret must be extracted from its own env file with a `sed -n` extraction rather than typed into a `read -rs` inside a pasted block, which consumes the next pasted line as its input; and env-file keys must be listed with a pattern that admits digits, because a letters-only pattern silently skips every `S3_…` line.

The `machinectl shell <user>@` requirement is not confined to bring-up: `systemctl --user` and the rootless `docker` CLI both need that user's systemd session (`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, its D-Bus, and the daemon's socket), so every later operation as `prod` — stopping the Nx-cache service, bringing a compose up, enabling a user unit — goes through `sudo machinectl shell prod@` rather than `sudo -iu prod`, which creates none of those and leaves `systemctl --user` failing and `docker` unable to find the daemon.

The host backup script's dump list is the part of Phase 14 that must grow with the host: the original script captured only Forgejo, Komodo and the object-store/cache config directories and no application database at all, so a reboot that corrupted Forgejo's Postgres left Forgejo the only stateful service with a real backup. The standing rule drawn from that incident is that whenever a stateful service is added its dump must be added to `backup.sh` — the same obligation that put the Nx-cache store's config directory on the `restic backup` path list.

The object-store migration ran ON the host, from a repository checkout, through the `scripts/object-store-migration.sh` wrapper: the host has no `node`, so the wrapper copied the Docker CLI out of a digest-pinned CLI image, ran the tool in a digest-pinned node container with the host's rootless Docker socket mounted, copied the tool and the git-tracked observability compose into it (no bind mount of a checkout path), and copied the evidence directory back out — and it refused `copy` without `--apply` before any container existed and refused `rehearse` outright. Credentials reached it by NAME (`-e S3_ACCESS_KEY -e S3_SECRET_KEY`) from the operator's shell, never as command-line values, and the tool was documented as never to be driven from the dev container over `DOCKER_HOST=ssh://`, because that would put standing root-equivalent control of the prod daemon in the sandbox. The tool and its wrapper were temporary by design: the cleanup PR (spec 080 T048, 2026-11-01) deleted `scripts/object-store-migration.mjs`, its two test files and `object-store-migration.sh`.

The migration tool refused rather than guessed, and its refusals were the safety property: `copy` required `--apply` (there was no dry-run spelling — `inventory` was how you looked), a target volume that already existed was refused rather than written into, a source volume still mounted by a running container was refused until the store was stopped, an `inventory` whose search instrument failed its self-test was refused (a BusyBox `grep` in its default locale misses markers inside a binary `xl.meta`, so a zero proved nothing), and a volume that did not exist was never created by looking at it. A passing copy recorded `targetPreexisted: false`, `entriesNotOwnedByRuntimeUid: 0`, and an unchanged source digest (a source that changed during the copy was reported as no longer a valid rollback target), and the copy chowned the target to the uid read from the pinned image rather than a hard-coded literal.

The migration tool's default helper image was not hard-coded: `--image` defaulted to the single digest-pinned `rustfs/rustfs` reference read out of the git-tracked observability prod compose (`infrastructure-as-code/docker/observability/compose.prod.yaml`), and the resolution errored if that file contained no such reference, more than one distinct reference, or a reference without a 64-hex `@sha256:` digest — so the uid the copy chowned to came from the real production pin. That resolution survives the tool's deletion as the `pinnedRustfsRef` helper inside `scripts/__tests__/object-store-service.guard.test.mjs`, which was the helper's only other consumer, and the guard still asserts the production compose carries one digest-pinned reference.

`scripts/__tests__/object-store-service.guard.test.mjs` enforces the RustFS service contract (specs/080-minio-to-rustfs/contracts/object-store-service.md, S1–S9) over the three git-tracked RustFS composes — `observability/compose.yaml`, `observability/compose.prod.yaml` and `backups/compose.yaml` — including clause S9, that the prod data volume is `external: true` under its canonical name `observability-langfuse-rustfs-data`, and it asserts it actually found the server and init services in each file so a guard cannot pass by matching nothing. The host-managed Nx-cache compose under the `prod` user's home is outside that scan, so for it the external-volume property rests on the runbook and on the volume existing rather than on a CI gate.

The Phase 8 runbook snippet's RustFS pin lags the git-tracked one: it still shows `rustfs/rustfs:1.0.1@sha256:1803faef…` while the tracked RustFS composes have moved on — the observability prod compose now pins `rustfs/rustfs:1.0.4@sha256:ed9210d6411d77ffceb70d94b964a3cb7d225983368bc25bebe01e995293dcc2`, and every git-tracked RustFS service (observability, observability prod and backups) must share that one digest-pinned Alpine tag. The host-managed Nx-cache compose is invisible to Renovate, so the pin must be copied by hand from the tracked file whenever that moves — check the tracked compose rather than the runbook's example.

A compose `up` that aborts on a missing external volume is loud rather than destructive: measured 2026-10-11 in the dev container against the shipped observability prod compose (Docker Compose 5.6.0, with every other external volume present so the RustFS one was the only gap, with and without pulling), compose aborted with `external volume "…" not found`, created zero containers, did not create the volume — and a scratch project showed the previously deployed containers were left running and unchanged, so a merge that lands before the copy leaves the old store still serving while the operator recovers.

The prod host backup is no longer host-only state: spec 084 (2026-10-27) moved it into `infrastructure-as-code/backup/`, which is now the source of truth (`backup.sh`, `backup-alert.sh`, `backup-staleness.sh`, the five systemd units, a README carrying the install/update/verify contract, and `INSTALLED.sha256`), while the host runs copies installed at the README's `$HOME`-relative paths. `cd ~ && sha256sum -c <checkout>/infrastructure-as-code/backup/INSTALLED.sha256` is the operator's one-line proof that the installed copies match the repository, and the manifest is regenerated by `scripts/backup-install-manifest.mjs --write` with a test asserting the committed list is not stale — so a change to what gets dumped, what is excluded, or when the alert fires is a reviewed commit rather than an edit made on the host.

The tracked backup's dump list is eight dumps — `forge-db`, `forge-data`, `komodo`, `keycloak`, `agent-db`, `mc-service-mongo`, `bff-mongo` and `release-apks` — each written through `run_dump` so that one dump's failure leaves a marker and the remaining dumps and the upload still run, each checked in its own format against a per-dump minimum (and against the previous run's size), with every verdict written into a `dump-manifest.tsv` that travels inside the snapshot. `forge-data` is deliberately an uncompressed tar rather than a gzip stream: restic de-duplicates an unchanged file but never a gzip stream, so the old `forgejo dump --type tar.gz` added 19.8–21.1 GiB to the repository every night, where an uncompressed tar of mostly-unchanged files adds roughly the day's real change.

Komodo's dump excludes the rows of `cron.job_run_details` — pg_cron's own run history, 11.9 M rows and 2,147 MB by 2026-10-27 with no job purging it, about 89,000 rows a day from DocumentDB's own jobs — and `komodo-cron-retention.sql` installs an hourly pg_cron job (`purge-cron-run-history`) that deletes runs older than 3 days. The dump carries a 500 MB maximum as well as a minimum, so the history returning alerts `komodo-oversize` and still uploads rather than silently re-inflating the snapshot.

The backup's silent-failure design rests on three independent mechanisms, each added because the script failed every night from 2026-07-27 to 2026-10-22 without anyone being told: staging is on disk and the script refuses a tmpfs staging directory (`/tmp` on this host is a 29 G tmpfs, and the forge dump — then still carrying the 100 G+ registry — outgrew it with `write /dev/stdout: no space left on device`); the service's `OnFailure=` runs `backup-alert.sh` for a failed run, and its 2 h `TimeoutStartSec` turns a hung run into a failure reported as `hung`; and a separate 6-hourly staleness check reads the newest snapshot from the repository itself and alerts `stale` past 36 h (or `staleness-unreadable` when it cannot tell, because "could not tell" is never "fresh"), catching a run that never happened or an upload that silently did nothing. Every event lands on one backlog item, `Prod backup: failed or stale`, which only a human closes.

The post-spec-084 backup format is proven on this host, not pending: the runbook's "Restore the forge (the format since spec 084 US4)" procedure — `forge-db` as a `pg_dump -Fc` custom dump (dependency-ordered, so one `pg_restore` pass suffices) plus the uncompressed `forge-data` tar — is headed as *Proven by the restore drill of 2026-10-31 (FR-006)*, and the drill log carries the passing row for snapshot `443ebb58` (forge-db 14 s, 0 errors, 2 repos / 1 user matching live; forge-data 23 s with `fsck ok=2 bad=0`; mc-service-mongo 2 s, 2,315 documents across 2 collections). The only restore proven before that drill was the old `forgejo dump` format (2026-07-05), whose xorm-generated SQL is not dependency-ordered and is therefore loaded twice with errors ignored — that procedure stays documented because old-format snapshots remain inside restic's retention window — and the drill log, not CI, is what records which format has actually been restored.

The restore drill (spec 084 FR-006) restores `forge-db`, `forge-data` and `mc-service-mongo` into scratch containers and a scratch directory and never touches a live service — the scratch containers run with `--network none`, and every block reads the live containers only to copy their image or count their rows. It must **not** run between 03:00 and 04:00, because restic's `forget --prune` needs an exclusive lock, so a drill still reading at 03:30 fails that night's backup run loudly through the alert. It wants about 2 GB free under `~/backup` and downloads about 1.5 GB from the NAS, and the runbook's rule is to run it after any change to what the backup carries and at least quarterly.

The post-spec-084 backup format is also much faster: a whole nightly run takes about 65 s (2026-10-29), against 8–10 min with the old `forgejo dump` (2026-10-22..26), because the forge is now a custom-format database dump plus an uncompressed data tar rather than one large `tar.gz`.

OCI-registry retention (spec 084 US5) is a repository script, `scripts/registry-retention.mjs`, configured by the tracked `infrastructure-as-code/forgejo/registry-retention.yaml` and run weekly by `.forgejo/workflows/registry-retention.yml` (Sundays 06:00 UTC, after the Friday Renovate window and outside the nightly backup). It exists instead of the forge's built-in package-cleanup rules because those match versions by name regex and so cannot protect a digest that a git file names, live only in the forge's web UI, and have no report-only run; the script computes every protection from git before its first API call, and refuses a config that is silently half-read (an unknown key, a duplicate package, `keepAll` together with a window, or a mode other than `report`/`apply`).

Registry retention keeps each version by the FIRST reason that applies and deletes it otherwise: `keep:protected` for a digest pinned in an `infrastructure-as-code/docker/*/.env.deploy` at the newest promotion or one of the 5 before it (the deployed set plus the rollback targets, because a rollback is a `git revert` of a promotion commit, read from git history before any API call); `keep:newest`/`keep:recent` for the newest `keepNewest` tags or anything younger than `keepDays` (the six app images 40 / 30 days, `mcm-devcontainer` 4 / 21); `keep:referenced` for a `sha256:` child a kept index points at, whatever its age; `keep:all` for `mcm-app-android`, whose release APKs are not rebuildable; and `keep:unconfigured` for a package absent from the config, which is reported and never deleted.

Registry-retention children are kept by reference rather than by age, because one push creates two kinds of version — the tag `<sha>`, whose `manifest.json` IS the digest `.env.deploy` pins (an OCI image index), and the `sha256:` children that index references (the platform manifest that owns the layers, plus an attestation) — and an unchanged image reuses a previous push's platform manifest. Measured 2026-10-31: on `mc-service` the 07:48 deployed index pointed at a platform manifest created at 03:14 by an earlier push, so deleting by age would delete the layers of the running image. A child is therefore kept while any kept index references it, and when any kept index cannot be read no child of that package is deleted at all (`keep:unverified`).

Three protections the registry-retention script enforces: it refuses a shallow clone because the rollback targets are read from git history, which is why the workflow checks out with `fetch-depth: 0`; when a protected digest is not found in the registry it exits 5 and deletes nothing, an alarm meaning a deployed or rollback image is gone or the pin is wrong; and on an apply it deletes indexes before their children, so no index surviving a partial run points at a deleted child.

Registry retention's report -> review -> apply flow needs two independent keys held in two places: the weekly schedule and any dispatch without `apply: true` are report-only, while deleting additionally requires `mode: apply` in the committed config — a one-line PR that links the reviewed report — plus a `registry-retention` dispatch with `apply: true`. The schedule never passes `--apply` and the script refuses `--apply` while the config says `report`, so the flip itself has since been made (the config now reads `mode: apply`) and a delete today is the dispatch alone; the guards remain the property the flip rests on. A reviewer checks that no `delete` row's `digest` appears in any `.env.deploy` of the last 6 promotions, and the report's byte total is an upper bound because a blob shared with a kept version is not freed — real storage returns only when the forge's own package-cleanup cron removes unreferenced blobs, so `du -sh` of the package store is checked after that has run rather than right after an apply.

The registry-retention apply runs with its own token: the workflow reads `REGISTRY_CLEANUP_TOKEN`, a forge token scoped `write:package` only (token `registry-cleanup` in the runbook's least-privilege inventory), deliberately separate from `actions-ci-push` so rotating either cannot break the other; a report is satisfiable with any read token, and the workflow falls back to a commit status when the digest's forge token is absent on an AGit-headed run.

The dev-container image's digest is pinned only in each developer's gitignored `MCM_DEVCONTAINER_IMAGE`, so no `.env.deploy` names it and `keep:protected` can never cover it — which is exactly why `mcm-devcontainer` keeps 4 / 21 days against the app images' 40 / 30, and why a stale pin must be refreshed from the newest `devcontainer-image` run within 21 days. Two further retention floors live in the same config: `ci-failures` bundles are pruned by `ci-failure-digest.mjs` itself at 30 days, so the config's entry only enforces the floor `ci-status durations` needs (25 runs multiplied by every bundle-publishing job, counted from the workflows, with `keepDays` not below `evidenceWindowDays`), and the Actions-artifact shelf is capped server-side by `FORGEJO__actions__ARTIFACT_RETENTION_DAYS=30` as the backstop for any upload without its own `retention-days` (the forge default is 90), while this repository's uploads set 14 (a diagnostic) or 7 (the APK, which also lives in the `mcm-app-android` package) — honoured by Forgejo 15, verified 2026-10-31.

The registry-retention config's committed `mode` is now `apply` (it read `report` for the first report-only run), and that value cannot be set without a reviewed report behind it: the config's own header names the report-only run and the backlog item it was reviewed on (`mode: apply` since the first report, run 6350, reviewed on item #863), and `scripts/__tests__/registry-retention.test.mjs` fails the build when the mode is `apply` and that header line is absent (FR-023). `scripts/__tests__/no-minio-references.guard.test.mjs` is what keeps the rename from decaying: it matches every git-tracked file's **path and content** case-insensitively against `/minio/` and fails naming `path:line`, against a closed list of reasoned exemptions; it proves it read the tree rather than a handful of files (a scanned-file floor); and it fails a stale exemption that matches no file or line, exactly as the allowlist gate fails an unmatched entry. A runbook case study may keep its evidence only between `<!-- history:begin -->` and `<!-- history:end -->`, honoured under `docs/runbooks/**` only and never as an excuse made in a comment, and an unclosed block does not exempt the rest of the file.
